title: Listening in Bairari
hook: a tiny raga, a few hymns, easy to hear whole

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Bairari, whose first hymn says sun man, listen, mind. Your line: small and bright.

The Guru Granth Sahib is easy to meet in pieces. One shabad in the morning. A hukamnama, the day's reading opened at random. A few lines sung in kirtan, then the next raga, the next Guru, the next page. A book this large invites that. Bairari offers something else: a whole section you can take in at once, start to finish, without losing the thread. A few hymns, a short stretch of pages, and then it's done. Today: listening in Bairari, all of it.
screen: `USUALLY IN PIECES.` → `ONE SHABAD, ONE HUKAMNAMA.` → `A WHOLE SECTION AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: It begins where yesterday left off, with Guru Ram Das: sun man, listen, mind, to the untellable story of the Lord's Name. More of his hymns follow, turning the same light around. One has a refrain worth carrying out of the room. It opens: har jan ram naam gun gaavai. In paraphrase: the Lord's servant sings the praises of the Name; and if anyone slanders that servant, the servant doesn't lose their own goodness. Slander is aimed at someone, but here it can't take anything from them. The goodness stays where it was. Then the voice changes. Guru Arjan, mahala five, closes the section, and his hymn moves from the single listener to a crowd: in paraphrase, the saints met together and sang the Lord's praise, and the pains of countless lifetimes went away. Hear the whole arc. A mind told to listen. A servant who can't be robbed of goodness by someone else's words. A gathering, singing together. Alone, then under pressure, then a sangat. Read one hymn and you get a line. Read all of Bairari and you get a little journey, from listening alone to singing together: the whole of it.
screen: `FIRST: LISTEN, MIND.` · `SLANDER CAN'T TAKE THE GOODNESS.` · `GURU ARJAN: THE SAINTS SING TOGETHER.` · `ALONE, UNDER PRESSURE, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE OF IT.`

segments.voice: If you have a Gurbani app or a printed Granth with meanings, read the Bairari pages straight through, slowly, or play its shabads one after another. Then sit and hold the shape of it, listening, steadiness, singing together, the way you'd hold a short letter after reading it, without picking a favorite line; if you pray, say Waheguru at the end.
Listening in Bairari. The short raga heard whole: a mind told to listen, a servant slander can't rob, and the saints singing together. Today's word.
Your line: the whole of it. Tomorrow, Raga Tilang, where the colors change again. Go gently.

howItsDone: Sikhs meet the Granth in daily shabads, in the hukamnama read at random each day, and in kirtan; some also read whole sections or the whole Granth through, and a short raga like Bairari can be read in one sitting.

chat.says: Why read a whole raga section at once instead of one shabad?
options: Heard whole, it has a shape: listening, steadiness under slander, then singing together.
Because single shabads don't count for anything unless the whole section is read.
Because Bairari has no single shabad that is worth singing on its own.

notes: All three hymns are paraphrased. Please confirm 'Har jan ram naam gun gaavai / je koi nind kare har jan ki apuna gun na gavaavai' is in Bairari Mahala 4 (Ang 719) and the paraphrase is fair.

Please confirm that Guru Arjan's single Bairari hymn is 'Sant jana mil har jas gaaio' (Ang 720), that it closes the section, and that 'the pains of countless lifetimes went away' fairly renders it ('kot janam ke dookh', given without a number).
The hook's 'easy to meet in pieces' and howItsDone's 'some also read whole sections' describe general practice without counts; please confirm.
